claim: Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth.
source: Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) constitutes the basis for one of the world's most important commercial fisheries (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Statistics Division, 2013) and has been a valuable food resource throughout human history in North Europe. It is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth with a total estimated breeding stock of one trillion individuals (Feng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2017 providing the population estimate.

claim: Atlantic herring has a total estimated breeding stock of one trillion individuals.
source: It is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth with a total estimated breeding stock of one trillion individuals (Feng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2017.

claim: Atlantic herring's short-term effective population size is enormous.
source: Its short-term (<10,000 years) effective population size is enormous whereas the long-term effective population size is much more restricted most likely due to the impact of periods of glaciation (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: Atlantic herring's long-term effective population size is much more restricted most likely due to the impact of periods of glaciation.
source: Its short-term (<10,000 years) effective population size is enormous whereas the long-term effective population size is much more restricted most likely due to the impact of periods of glaciation (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016 and inference about glaciation impact.

claim: Genetic draft contributes to restricting nucleotide diversity in Atlantic herring.
source: It is likely that genetic draft (Walsh and Lynch, 2018) that is purging of neutral genetic variation linked to polymorphisms under positive or negative selection, also contributes to restricting nucleotide diversity in the herring.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walsh and Lynch, 2018 and inference about genetic draft effects.

claim: Atlantic herring has a nucleotide diversity of approximately 0.3%.
source: As a consequence, the nucleotide diversity is moderate (~0.3%) (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016), only three-fold higher than in human although the census population size is at least two orders of magnitude higher in herring at present and until recently (>1,000 years ago) many orders of magnitude higher.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: Atlantic herring's nucleotide diversity is only three-fold higher than in human.
source: As a consequence, the nucleotide diversity is moderate (~0.3%) (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016), only three-fold higher than in human although the census population size is at least two orders of magnitude higher in herring at present and until recently (>1,000 years ago) many orders of magnitude higher.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016 and comparison with human.

claim: Atlantic herring has adapted to the brackish Baltic Sea where salinity drops to 2–3 PSU.
source: The herring has adapted to different marine environments including the brackish Baltic Sea, where salinity drops to 2–3 PSU and water temperature shows a much larger variation among seasons than in the Atlantic Ocean with typically 34–35 PSU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing environmental conditions.

claim: There is minute genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci among herring populations from different geographic regions.
source: There is minute genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci among herring populations from different geographic regions (Lamichhaney et al., 2012; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) and the distribution of per locus FST values deviates significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral loci with an excessive number of outlier loci demonstrating signatures of selection (Lamichhaney et al., 2017; Limborg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lamichhaney et al., 2012 and Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: The distribution of per locus FST values in herring deviates significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral loci with an excessive number of outlier loci demonstrating signatures of selection.
source: There is minute genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci among herring populations from different geographic regions (Lamichhaney et al., 2012; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) and the distribution of per locus FST values deviates significantly from the one expected for selectively neutral loci with an excessive number of outlier loci demonstrating signatures of selection (Lamichhaney et al., 2017; Limborg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lamichhaney et al., 2017 and Limborg et al., 2012.

claim: The study performed pooled whole-genome sequencing using 28 population samples of Atlantic herring.
source: We performed pooled whole-genome sequencing using 28 population samples of Atlantic herring.
evidence: Direct statement about the study methodology.

claim: The study analyzed a total of 53 population samples including previously published data.
source: These were analyzed together with previously published data (Lamichhaney et al., 2017; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016), making a total number of 53 population samples.
evidence: Direct statement about the total sample size combining new and published data.

claim: The 53 population samples cover the entire species distribution and include spring, autumn, winter and summer spawning populations.
source: Together the 53 population samples cover the entire species distribution and include spring, autumn, winter and summer spawning populations (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The study identified approximately 11.5 million polymorphic biallelic sites among the 53 population samples.
source: In total, we identified ~11.5 million polymorphic biallelic sites among the 53 population samples and ~15.9 million sites when including Pacific herring.
evidence: Direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: The study identified approximately 15.9 million polymorphic biallelic sites when including Pacific herring.
source: In total, we identified ~11.5 million polymorphic biallelic sites among the 53 population samples and ~15.9 million sites when including Pacific herring.
evidence: Direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: The 53 population samples group into seven primary clusters based on genome-wide SNPs.
source: A genetic distance tree, based on genome-wide SNPs, groups the 53 population samples into seven primary clusters: (i) autumn- and (ii) spring-spawning herring from the brackish Baltic Sea, (iii) populations from the transition zone, close to the entrance to the Baltic Sea, spawning at lower salinity than in the Atlantic Ocean, (iv) Norwegian fjord populations, (v) populations around Ireland and Britain, (vi) autumn- and (vii) spring-spawning herring from the North Atlantic Ocean (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing the genetic distance tree.

claim: Pairwise FST values among all populations are in the range 0.013 to 0.061.
source: Pairwise FST values among all populations are in the range 0.013 to 0.061 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PCA based on 169,394 undifferentiated markers explained only approximately 11% of the variance in the first two principal components.
source: The first two principal components in this analysis explained only ~11% of the variance.
evidence: Direct statement of PCA results.

claim: PCA based on 794 markers showing the most striking genetic differentiation separated the populations into seven main clusters.
source: In contrast, the PCA based on only 794 markers showing the most striking genetic differentiation separated the populations into the seven main clusters (Figure 2b), consistent with the genetic distance tree (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first principal component in the PCA based on 794 differentiated markers explained 43% of the variance.
source: The first principal component explained 43% of the variance.
evidence: Direct statement of PCA results.

claim: The observed population structure in herring can be accounted for by a small fraction of genetic markers associated with loci underlying ecological adaptation.
source: These two patterns observed for the two sets of markers suggest that the observed population structure in herring can be accounted for by a small fraction of genetic markers associated with loci underlying ecological adaptation.
evidence: Inference based on the comparison of PCA results from differentiated and undifferentiated markers.

claim: Two population samples from Landvikvannet in southern Norway clustered more closely with populations from the transition zone than with local fjord populations from western Norway.
source: Two population samples (#24 and 25) both from Landvikvannet in southern Norway clustered more closely with populations from the transition zone than with local fjord populations from western Norway.
evidence: Direct observation from PCA analysis.

claim: Landvikvannet is a unique brackish lake created in 1877 by opening a canal between the ocean and a freshwater lake.
source: Landvikvannet is a unique brackish lake created in 1877 by opening a canal between the ocean and a freshwater lake, now harboring a local population of herring adapted to this brackish environment (Eggers et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eggers et al., 2014.

claim: One population from Schlei collected as autumn-spawning clustered with spring-spawning populations.
source: One of the populations from Schlei (#21), collected as autumn-spawning, clustered with spring-spawning populations.
evidence: Direct observation from PCA analysis.

claim: Otolith examinations showed that the Schlei autumn-spawning sample actually hatched in spring.
source: Interestingly, examinations of the otoliths from fish in this sample, using the method by Clausen et al., 2007, showed that they hatched in spring!
evidence: Supported by data from otolith examination and citation to Clausen et al., 2007 for the method.

claim: The Schlei sample represents a group of herring that has switched spawning season from spring to autumn.
source: Thus, this must represent a group of herring that has switched spawning season from spring to autumn, maybe because their nutritional status was insufficient to support spawning (McQuinn, 1997), demonstrating that spawning time in herring is controlled by a combination of genetic and environmental factors (Bekkevold et al., 2007; Berg et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference based on otolith data, supported by citations to McQuinn, 1997; Bekkevold et al., 2007; and Berg et al., 2020.

claim: Spawning time in herring is controlled by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.
source: Thus, this must represent a group of herring that has switched spawning season from spring to autumn, maybe because their nutritional status was insufficient to support spawning (McQuinn, 1997), demonstrating that spawning time in herring is controlled by a combination of genetic and environmental factors (Bekkevold et al., 2007; Berg et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bekkevold et al., 2007 and Berg et al., 2020.

claim: The Baltic/Northeast Atlantic contrast using spring-spawning populations resulted in 115 loci reaching statistical significance.
source: The Baltic/Northeast Atlantic contrast using 19 spring-spawning and 9 autumn-spawning populations resulted in a total number of 115 and 39 loci, respectively, reaching statistical significance (Figure 3a; results for individual chromosomes are in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and all highly differentiated SNPs are listed in Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 3a and supplementary materials.

claim: The Baltic/Northeast Atlantic contrast using autumn-spawning populations resulted in 39 loci reaching statistical significance.
source: The Baltic/Northeast Atlantic contrast using 19 spring-spawning and 9 autumn-spawning populations resulted in a total number of 115 and 39 loci, respectively, reaching statistical significance (Figure 3a; results for individual chromosomes are in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and all highly differentiated SNPs are listed in Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 3a and supplementary materials.

claim: 30 loci reached significance in both spring and autumn Baltic/Northeast Atlantic comparisons.
source: As many as 30 of these loci reached significance in both comparisons (highlighted in red in Figure 3a).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 3a.

claim: LRRC8C is a candidate for adaptation to the environmental conditions in the brackish Baltic Sea irrespective of spawning time.
source: These loci are the best candidates for adaptation to the environmental conditions in the brackish Baltic Sea irrespective of spawning time. A prime example of such a locus is LRRC8C (leucine-rich repeat-containing 8 protein, subunit C) (p<10−72, in spring-spawners and p<10−37 in autumn-spawners) which encodes a volume-regulated anion-channel.
evidence: Supported by statistical significance values and known gene function.

claim: LRRC8C encodes a volume-regulated anion-channel.
source: A prime example of such a locus is LRRC8C (leucine-rich repeat-containing 8 protein, subunit C) (p<10−72, in spring-spawners and p<10−37 in autumn-spawners) which encodes a volume-regulated anion-channel.
evidence: Statement of known gene function.

claim: PRLR is highly significant in both replicate Baltic/Northeast Atlantic comparisons.
source: Another locus that was highly significant in both replicate comparisons is PRLR (prolactin receptor) on Chr12 highlighted in Figure 3b.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3b.

claim: The most significant association at the PRLR locus is a cluster of non-coding SNPs located in a gene desert upstream of PRLR.
source: The most significant association at this locus is a cluster of non-coding SNPs located in a gene desert upstream of PRLR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: PRLR has a critical role for osmoregulation and adaptation to salinity in fish.
source: This hormone-receptor has an important role during lactation in mammals and a critical role for osmoregulation and adaptation to salinity in fish (Manzon, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manzon, 2002.

claim: A large 7.8 Mb region on Chr12 shows very strong genetic differentiation between autumn-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring but no genetic differentiation in spring-spawning contrast.
source: A striking example of such a locus is the large 7.8 Mb region on Chr12 that shows no genetic differentiation in the spring-spawning contrast, but very strong genetic differentiation between autumn-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring (Figure 3b).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3b.

claim: The 7.8 Mb region on Chr12 corresponds to a recently reported inversion.
source: This region corresponds to a recently reported inversion (Pettersson et al., 2019) (see further data below).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pettersson et al., 2019.

claim: The spring-/autumn-spawning contrast in Baltic populations yielded 31 significant loci.
source: The spring-/autumn-spawning contrast involved 16 Baltic and 12 Northeast Atlantic populations, which yielded 31 and 13 significant loci, respectively (Figure 3c; results for individual chromosomes are in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and all highly differentiated SNPs are listed in Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 3c and supplementary materials.

claim: The spring-/autumn-spawning contrast in Northeast Atlantic populations yielded 13 significant loci.
source: The spring-/autumn-spawning contrast involved 16 Baltic and 12 Northeast Atlantic populations, which yielded 31 and 13 significant loci, respectively (Figure 3c; results for individual chromosomes are in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and all highly differentiated SNPs are listed in Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 3c and supplementary materials.

claim: Seven loci were significant in both Baltic and Northeast Atlantic spring-/autumn-spawning replicates.
source: Only seven loci were significant in both replicates.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results.

claim: Three of the seven replicated loci in the spring-/autumn-spawning contrast were found within 5 Mb on Chr15.
source: Out of the seven replicated loci, three were found within 5 Mb on Chr15 (Figure 3d).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3d.

claim: TSHR is the most significant signal among the replicated loci on Chr15 associated with spawning season.
source: The most significant signal among those contains the TSHR (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone-Receptor) locus (p<10−68 in Baltic populations and p<10−53 in Atlantic populations), which has a well-defined role in the pathway regulating seasonal reproduction in vertebrates (Nakane et al., 2013; Nakane and Yoshimura, 2019) and CALM1B (Calmodulin), which regulates gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signaling via the MAPK pathway (Melamed et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by statistical significance values and citations to Nakane et al., 2013; Nakane and Yoshimura, 2019; and Melamed et al., 2012.

claim: TSHR has a well-defined role in the pathway regulating seasonal reproduction in vertebrates.
source: The most significant signal among those contains the TSHR (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone-Receptor) locus (p<10−68 in Baltic populations and p<10−53 in Atlantic populations), which has a well-defined role in the pathway regulating seasonal reproduction in vertebrates (Nakane et al., 2013; Nakane and Yoshimura, 2019) and CALM1B (Calmodulin), which regulates gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signaling via the MAPK pathway (Melamed et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakane et al., 2013 and Nakane and Yoshimura, 2019.

claim: CALM1B regulates gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signaling via the MAPK pathway.
source: The most significant signal among those contains the TSHR (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone-Receptor) locus (p<10−68 in Baltic populations and p<10−53 in Atlantic populations), which has a well-defined role in the pathway regulating seasonal reproduction in vertebrates (Nakane et al., 2013; Nakane and Yoshimura, 2019) and CALM1B (Calmodulin), which regulates gonadotrophin-releasing hormone signaling via the MAPK pathway (Melamed et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melamed et al., 2012.

claim: SOX11B plays an essential role in sex determination in zebrafish.
source: Another significant locus on Chr15 is SOX11B (SRY-Box Transcription Factor 11), which plays an essential role in sex determination in zebrafish (Santos et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2007.

claim: The most significant sequence variant at the SOX11B locus is a single-base change in a non-coding region located 39 kb upstream of SOX11B.
source: Notably, the most significant sequence variant at this locus (p<10−65 in Baltic populations and p<10−57 in Atlantic populations) is a single-base change in a non-coding region located 39 kb upstream of SOX11B (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that it may be a causal regulatory mutation.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2b and statistical significance values.

claim: The third highly significant locus on Chr15 contains ESR2A and SYNE2, which are only 100 kb apart.
source: The third highly significant locus on Chr15 contains ESR2A (Estrogen Receptor Beta) and SYNE2 (Spectrin Repeat Containing Nuclear Envelope 2), and these two genes are only 100 kb apart (Figure 3d).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3d.

claim: A premature stop codon in SYNE2 causes defects in photoreceptors in mice.
source: However, SYNE2 encodes an important structural protein and a premature stop codon in this gene is reported to cause defects in photoreceptors in mice (Maddox et al., 2015), suggesting that it may in fact have a role in photoperiod regulation of reproduction in herring.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maddox et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple members of MYHC gene family on Chr12 are associated with adaptation to different spawning seasons.
source: In addition to the signals on Chr15, we also found other loci that are associated with adaptation to different spawning seasons, such as multiple members of MYHC (myosin heavy chain) gene family on Chr12, which may be related to a reported association between myogenesis and plasticity of seasonal development in herring (Johnston et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnston et al., 2001.

claim: The contrast between Ireland/Britain populations and neighboring Northeast Atlantic populations found 12 independent loci showing significant genetic differentiation.
source: We grouped 10 populations from this region as one superpool, and compared its genome-wide allele frequency with another superpool, which consisted of 4 neighboring populations from the Northeast Atlantic Ocean (Figure 4a). Following the definition of independent loci (see Methods), we found only 12 independent loci showing significant genetic differentiation in this contrast.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results, supported by Figure 4a.

claim: Four major loci on Chr6, 12, 17, and 23 span exceptionally large regions.
source: However, four of the major loci on Chr6, 12, 17, and 23 span exceptionally large regions on four different chromosomes (Figure 4a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4a.

claim: The zoom-in profile of the significant SNPs at each of the four major loci formed a block-like pattern with sharp changes of divergence at borders.
source: Unlike a typical selective sweep where divergence of the markers forms a bell shape, the zoom-in profile of the significant SNPs at each locus formed a block-like pattern, where a sharp change of divergence was observed at borders (Figure 4b–e).
evidence: Direct observation supported by Figure 4b–e.

claim: The block-like patterns are consistent with the presence of inversions or other structural rearrangements.
source: The block-like patterns, suggesting suppressed recombination, are consistent with the presence of inversions or other structural rearrangements.
evidence: Inference based on observed patterns.

claim: The majority of populations from Ireland and Britain tend to be homozygous for S haplotypes while N haplotypes dominate in all other populations at the putative structural variants.
source: Further exploration of allele frequencies at diagnostic markers at each putative structural variant showed that the majority of the populations from Ireland and Britain tend to be homozygous for S (South) haplotypes while N (North) haplotypes dominate in all other populations (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: At the Chr6 locus, all other Baltic and Atlantic populations tend to be fixed for the N haplotype, except a few populations from Norwegian fjords and the transition zone.
source: At the Chr6 locus, all other Baltic and Atlantic populations tend to be fixed for the N haplotype, except a few populations from Norwegian fjords and the transition zone, which suggests that Chr6 S haplotype is contributing to adaptation to local ecological conditions around Ireland and Britain, and occurs at a particularly high frequency in populations spawning near the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, the Downs near the English Channel and in the Celtic Sea (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The Chr12 inversion is potentially associated with adaptation to water temperature at spawning or at the larval stage over the winter months.
source: In fact, it coincides with a recently reported inversion, which is potentially associated with adaptation to water temperature at spawning (Pettersson et al., 2019) or at the larval stage over the winter months (Fuentes-Pardo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pettersson et al., 2019 and Fuentes-Pardo et al., 2019.

claim: Recombinant versions of the Chr12 inversion are frequent in the Baltic Sea.
source: The individual sequence data reveal that recombinant versions of this inversion are frequent in the Baltic Sea, but the exact breakpoints of the recombined regions within the inversion are variable (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both N and S haplotypes at each of the four loci show lower nucleotide diversity than the genome average.
source: We found that, in general, both N and S haplotypes at each locus show lower nucleotide diversity in the range 0.11% to 0.31% than the genome average (~0.3%) and S haplotypes tend to be more variable than N haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: S haplotypes tend to be more variable than N haplotypes at the four putative inversion loci.
source: We found that, in general, both N and S haplotypes at each locus show lower nucleotide diversity in the range 0.11% to 0.31% than the genome average (~0.3%) and S haplotypes tend to be more variable than N haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genetic recombination has been restricted between N and S haplotypes at the four putative inversion loci.
source: This suggests that genetic recombination has been restricted between haplotypes and that N haplotypes are younger than the S haplotypes or have been more affected by population bottlenecks, possibly before or during the last glaciation.
evidence: Inference based on nucleotide diversity patterns.

claim: The most striking signal of selection in the contrast involving North Atlantic herring is a locus on Chr2 overlapping AHR2B2.
source: However, the most striking signal of selection in the contrast involving the North Atlantic herring is a locus on Chr2 overlapping a single gene: Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor 2B2 (AHR2B2) (Figure 5a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5a.

claim: Four of the ten top SNPs at the AHR2B2 locus are missense mutations.
source: Four of the ten top SNPs at this locus are missense mutations, including the one (Ser346Thr) that by far showed the strongest genetic differentiation (p<10−45; Figure 5b), suggesting that it is likely to be a causal variant.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5b and statistical significance value.

claim: The Ser346Thr missense mutation in AHR2B2 is likely to be a causal variant.
source: Four of the ten top SNPs at this locus are missense mutations, including the one (Ser346Thr) that by far showed the strongest genetic differentiation (p<10−45; Figure 5b), suggesting that it is likely to be a causal variant.
evidence: Inference based on statistical significance and mutation type, supported by Figure 5b.

claim: The non-reference allele Thr346 occurs at a high frequency in all population samples from the North Atlantic Ocean.
source: The non-reference allele Thr346 occurs at a high frequency in all population samples from the North Atlantic Ocean whereas the reference allele Ser346 dominates in all other population samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The most significant SNP on Chr7 is located approximately 1 kb upstream of SLA12A2/NKCC1.
source: The most significant SNP on Chr7 (p<10−24; Figure 5a) is located ~1 kb upstream of solute carrier family 12 (sodium/chloride transporter) member 2 (SLA12A2/NKCC1), a gene that shows altered expression in response to changes in salinity in spawning sea lamprey (Ferreira-Martins et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5a and citation to Ferreira-Martins et al., 2016.

claim: SLA12A2/NKCC1 shows altered expression in response to changes in salinity in spawning sea lamprey.
source: The most significant SNP on Chr7 (p<10−24; Figure 5a) is located ~1 kb upstream of solute carrier family 12 (sodium/chloride transporter) member 2 (SLA12A2/NKCC1), a gene that shows altered expression in response to changes in salinity in spawning sea lamprey (Ferreira-Martins et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira-Martins et al., 2016.

claim: Mutations in THRB cause generalized thyroid hormone resistance in human.
source: Another interesting locus is THRB (thyroid hormone-receptor beta) on Chr19 encoding a medically important nuclear receptor. Mutations in THRB cause generalized thyroid hormone resistance in human (Ferrara et al., 2012) and a recent CRISPR study in zebrafish revealed its function in photoreceptor development (Deveau et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferrara et al., 2012.

claim: A recent CRISPR study in zebrafish revealed THRB's function in photoreceptor development.
source: Another interesting locus is THRB (thyroid hormone-receptor beta) on Chr19 encoding a medically important nuclear receptor. Mutations in THRB cause generalized thyroid hormone resistance in human (Ferrara et al., 2012) and a recent CRISPR study in zebrafish revealed its function in photoreceptor development (Deveau et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deveau et al., 2019.

claim: At the herring THRB locus, all populations from high salinity conditions are fixed for an Atlantic haplotype.
source: At the herring THRB locus, all populations from high salinity conditions (34–35 PSU) are fixed for an Atlantic haplotype whereas, with a few exceptions, a 'Baltic' haplotype, which must have been introgressed from the sister species Pacific herring, dominates in all populations from the Baltic Sea, the transition zone and Norwegian fjords (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A 'Baltic' haplotype at THRB must have been introgressed from the sister species Pacific herring.
source: At the herring THRB locus, all populations from high salinity conditions (34–35 PSU) are fixed for an Atlantic haplotype whereas, with a few exceptions, a 'Baltic' haplotype, which must have been introgressed from the sister species Pacific herring, dominates in all populations from the Baltic Sea, the transition zone and Norwegian fjords (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inference based on haplotype distribution, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The only sequence difference between the introgressed THRB haplotype and the haplotype present in Pacific herring from Vancouver is a missense mutation Gln40His.
source: The only sequence difference between this introgressed haplotype and the haplotype present in Pacific herring from Vancouver is a missense mutation in THRB, Gln40His.
evidence: Direct statement of sequence comparison results.

claim: PacBio long read sequencing provided conclusive evidence for the presence of inversions on Chr6 and 17.
source: PacBio sequencing provided conclusive evidence for the presence of inversions on Chr6 and 17 (Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6.

claim: On Chr6, the distal breakpoint is at 24,868,581 bp.
source: On Chr6, the distal breakpoint is at 24,868,581 bp and the proximal breakpoint lies between 22,280,036 bp and 22,290,000 bp.
evidence: Direct statement of PacBio sequencing results.

claim: On Chr6, the proximal breakpoint lies between 22,280,036 bp and 22,290,000 bp.
source: On Chr6, the distal breakpoint is at 24,868,581 bp and the proximal breakpoint lies between 22,280,036 bp and 22,290,000 bp.
evidence: Direct statement of PacBio sequencing results.

claim: On Chr17, the proximal breakpoint is at 25,805,445 bp and the distal breakpoint is at 27,568,511 bp.
source: There are 36 reads supporting this pattern with 25,805,445 bp as the proximal breakpoint and 27,568,511 bp as the distal breakpoint.
evidence: Direct statement of PacBio sequencing results.

claim: A 5 kb duplicated sequence is present in the reference N haplotype at the Chr17 inversion, located with an opposite orientation at the two breakpoints.
source: The inserted dotplot shows the presence of a 5 kb duplicated sequence in the reference N haplotype, located with an opposite orientation at the two breakpoints.
evidence: Direct observation from PacBio data analysis.

claim: The 5 kb sequence at the Chr17 inversion is present as a single copy in the S haplotype of the PacBio individual.
source: This 5 kb sequence is present as a single copy in the S haplotype of the PacBio individual, implying that the N haplotype is most likely the derived state, and that the inversion and duplication occurred during the same meiotic event.
evidence: Direct observation from PacBio data analysis.

claim: The N haplotype at the Chr17 inversion is most likely the derived state.
source: This 5 kb sequence is present as a single copy in the S haplotype of the PacBio individual, implying that the N haplotype is most likely the derived state, and that the inversion and duplication occurred during the same meiotic event.
evidence: Inference based on duplication pattern.

claim: The inversion and duplication at Chr17 occurred during the same meiotic event.
source: This 5 kb sequence is present as a single copy in the S haplotype of the PacBio individual, implying that the N haplotype is most likely the derived state, and that the inversion and duplication occurred during the same meiotic event.
evidence: Inference based on duplication pattern.

claim: There are 44 genes present within the inverted region of Chr6.
source: There is a total of 44 and 66 genes present within the inverted regions of Chr6 and 17, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of gene count.

claim: There are 66 genes present within the inverted region of Chr17.
source: There is a total of 44 and 66 genes present within the inverted regions of Chr6 and 17, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of gene count.

claim: The inversion breakpoints on Chr6 and Chr17 do not disrupt any coding sequence.
source: The inversion breakpoints do not disrupt any coding sequence, but the proximal breakpoint of the Chr6 inversion is located very close to exon 1 of the methyl transferase 3 (PRMT3) gene suggesting that the inversion might affect its expression pattern.
evidence: Direct statement of PacBio sequencing analysis results.

claim: The proximal breakpoint of the Chr6 inversion is located very close to exon 1 of PRMT3.
source: The inversion breakpoints do not disrupt any coding sequence, but the proximal breakpoint of the Chr6 inversion is located very close to exon 1 of the methyl transferase 3 (PRMT3) gene suggesting that the inversion might affect its expression pattern.
evidence: Direct statement of PacBio sequencing analysis results.

claim: PRMT3 is a highly conserved gene in vertebrates and involved in bone development in human.
source: It is a highly conserved gene in vertebrates and involved in bone development in human (Min et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Min et al., 2019.

claim: The first population genetic studies on Atlantic herring in the early 1980s revealed no significant allele frequency differences even between Atlantic and Baltic herring.
source: The first population genetic studies on Atlantic herring in the early 1980s were based on a dozen allozyme markers and revealed the unexpected result of no significant allele frequency differences even between Atlantic and Baltic herring considered as subspecies (Andersson et al., 1981; Ryman et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andersson et al., 1981 and Ryman et al., 1984.

claim: Sequence variants associated with ecological adaptation best reveal the population structure of the Atlantic herring.
source: An important practical implication of the current study is that sequence variants associated with ecological adaptation best reveal the population structure of the Atlantic herring (Figure 2b), whereas neutral markers are less useful for population identification (Figure 2a).
evidence: Inference based on PCA results, supported by Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: A PCA analysis based on about 800 SNPs can distinguish all major groups of Atlantic herring.
source: A PCA analysis based on only about 800 SNPs out of the more than 10 million SNPs detected in the study distinguish all major groups of Atlantic herring and reveal allele frequency differences between subpopulations within major groups.
evidence: Direct statement of PCA results.

claim: The Ser346Thr mutation in AHR alone can efficiently distinguish the North Atlantic Ocean groups from all other groups of herring.
source: For instance, the Ser346Thr mutation in AHR alone can efficiently distinguish the North Atlantic Ocean groups from all other groups of herring (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The genetic architecture underlying ecological adaptation in Atlantic herring is polygenic with the number of loci showing strong genetic differentiation in the hundreds.
source: The genetic architecture underlying ecological adaptation in Atlantic herring is strikingly different. It is polygenic but the number of loci showing strong genetic differentiation is in the hundreds and not in the thousands.
evidence: Inference based on the study's findings.

claim: The herring data deviates from the expected pattern under a strict infinitesimal model because this theory predicts that a response to natural selection should only cause minor changes in allele frequencies.
source: The herring data nevertheless deviates from the expected pattern under a strict infinitesimal model because this theory predicts that a response to natural selection should only cause minor changes in allele frequencies.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with theoretical expectations.

claim: The herring has adapted to the brackish Baltic Sea after it was formed about 10,000 years ago.
source: For instance, the herring has adapted to the brackish Baltic Sea after it was formed about 10,000 years ago (Andrén et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andrén et al., 2011.

claim: The genetic architecture underlying ecological adaptation in herring is similar to the genetic architecture underlying skin color in humans.
source: The genetic architecture underlying ecological adaptation in herring is in fact similar to the genetic architecture underlying skin color in humans, a trait affected by strong natural selection, for which four major loci were estimated to explain 35% of the total variance in an admixed population (Beleza et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beleza et al., 2013 and comparison with human skin color genetics.

claim: A missense mutation in rhodopsin (Phe261Tyr) has a critical role for adaptation to the red-shifted light conditions in the Baltic Sea.
source: A striking example concerns rhodopsin (RHO), showing strong genetic differentiation between Atlantic and Baltic herring (Figure 3a). A missense mutation in this gene (Phe261Tyr) has a critical role for adaptation to the red-shifted light conditions in the Baltic Sea (Hill et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hill et al., 2019 and Figure 3a.

claim: About one third of all fish adapted to red-shifted light conditions in freshwater and brackish water carry Tyr261 like the Baltic herring.
source: Interestingly, about one third of all fish adapted to red-shifted light conditions in freshwater and brackish water carry Tyr261 like the Baltic herring, an amazing example of convergent evolution (Hill et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hill et al., 2019.

claim: Thr346 must be the derived allele at the AHR2B2 locus since all tested Pacific herring were homozygous Ser346.
source: Thr346 must be the derived allele since all tested Pacific herring were homozygous Ser346.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with Pacific herring.

claim: Residue 346 in AHR2B2 is located in the highly conserved PAS-B domain.
source: Furthermore, residue 346 is located in the highly conserved PAS-B domain and Ser346 is highly conserved among vertebrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting a functional significance of Ser346Thr.
evidence: Supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1b showing conservation.

claim: Ser346 is highly conserved among vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, residue 346 is located in the highly conserved PAS-B domain and Ser346 is highly conserved among vertebrates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting a functional significance of Ser346Thr.
evidence: Supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1b showing conservation.

claim: A population of killifish has been able to colonize highly polluted waters due to the presence of a deletion knocking out AHR function.
source: It has recently been reported that a population of killifish has been able to colonize highly polluted waters due to the presence of a deletion knocking out AHR function (Oziolor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oziolor et al., 2019.

claim: The derived Thr346 allele occurs at a high frequency in the least polluted waters in the North Atlantic Ocean.
source: In herring, the derived Thr346 allele occurs at a high frequency in the least polluted waters in the North Atlantic Ocean, for example around Greenland and Iceland, suggesting that it is unlikely that this adaptation is related to the presence of exogenous metabolites.
evidence: Direct statement based on allele frequency data.

claim: Billions of herring in the North Atlantic Ocean are homozygous for Thr346.
source: Billions of herring in the North Atlantic Ocean are homozygous for Thr346 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The four inversion polymorphisms on Chr6, 12, 17, and 23 have characteristic features including that the inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequence.
source: The characteristic features of these four inversion polymorphisms are that (i) the inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequence (conclusive evidence only for Chr6 and 17 so far), (ii) no allele is lethal in the homozygous condition, (iii) the inversions suppress recombination but not completely, as we find evidence for recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and (iv) none of the inversions is of recent origin as indicated by substantial nucleotide diversity within each haplotype group, in the range 0.11–0.31% (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement of findings supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: No allele at the four inversion polymorphisms is lethal in the homozygous condition.
source: The characteristic features of these four inversion polymorphisms are that (i) the inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequence (conclusive evidence only for Chr6 and 17 so far), (ii) no allele is lethal in the homozygous condition, (iii) the inversions suppress recombination but not completely, as we find evidence for recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and (iv) none of the inversions is of recent origin as indicated by substantial nucleotide diversity within each haplotype group, in the range 0.11–0.31% (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inference based on observed homozygous individuals.

source: The characteristic features of these four inversion polymorphisms are that (i) the inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequence (conclusive evidence only for Chr6 and 17 so far), (ii) no allele is lethal in the homozygous condition, (iii) the inversions suppress recombination but not completely, as we find evidence for recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and (iv) none of the inversions is of recent origin as indicated by substantial nucleotide diversity within each haplotype group, in the range 0.11–0.31% (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing recombinant haplotypes.

claim: None of the four inversions is of recent origin as indicated by substantial nucleotide diversity within each haplotype group.
source: The characteristic features of these four inversion polymorphisms are that (i) the inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequence (conclusive evidence only for Chr6 and 17 so far), (ii) no allele is lethal in the homozygous condition, (iii) the inversions suppress recombination but not completely, as we find evidence for recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and (iv) none of the inversions is of recent origin as indicated by substantial nucleotide diversity within each haplotype group, in the range 0.11–0.31% (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inference based on nucleotide diversity data, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The strong genetic differentiation among populations for each of the four inversions implies that these are supergenes important for environmental adaptation.
source: The strong genetic differentiation among populations for each of the four inversions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) implies that these are supergenes important for environmental adaptation.
evidence: Inference based on genetic differentiation patterns, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ecological adaptation in the Atlantic herring is associated with large shifts in allele frequencies at loci under selection.
source: In conclusion, ecological adaptation in the Atlantic herring is associated with large shifts in allele frequencies at loci under selection.
evidence: Summary statement based on the study's findings.
